metadata.title: Palantir just posted a record quarter—so why did the stock sink?

content.text:
Investing.com and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.
Investing.com — The Nasdaq-100 slid into correction territory at the start of November as investors questioned whether Big Tech's AI spending will pay off, putting high-multiple AI names under pressure. ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW), growing revenue at 21.8%, lost 30.0% in the month to November 17. Yet even Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR)—the AI software company behind the Gotham, Foundry, and AIP platforms, which just posted its fastest growth as a public company—has tumbled 15.8% over the past month to $156.56, including a 9.2% slide in the past week alone.
Palantir's sell-off is not a verdict on its business but the market repricing a stock that had already paid in advance for years of that growth. Analysts forecast revenue growth of 90.7% and EPS growth of 188.8%, figures that make every dip look like an entry point. Even after the pullback, though, Palantir trades at 102.8 times trailing earnings, a multiple that leaves no margin for a slower quarter.
Identifying when a software leader's valuation has outrun even record growth is what ProPicks AI is built for. In Tech Titans, InvestingPro's strategy dedicated to high-margin tech leaders, Palantir lost out to cash-generative tech names trading at far lower multiples—including a wireless chip designer, a specialty chip foundry, and a PC and printer maker.
Palantir makes its money by turning short AI pilots into large production contracts on platforms that customers find hard to replace. Gotham, Foundry, and AIP are built on a proprietary data ontology that wires the software into mission-critical workflows, creating high switching costs once a deployment goes live. AIP bootcamps have shortened the path from pilot to production—in the third quarter, one $1 million pilot converted into a $15 million annual contract value deal within the same quarter.
Third-quarter results showed that model at record scale. Revenue surged 96% year-over-year to $2.31 billion, the first quarter above $2 billion, and adjusted EPS of $0.44 topped the $0.41 consensus. U.S. commercial revenue climbed 148% to $984 million and overtook U.S. government revenue of $953 million for the first time in company history. Net dollar retention reached 165%, up 800 basis points from the prior quarter.
That growth converts into cash. GAAP net income reached $1.13 billion, a 49% margin, adjusted operating margin hit 62%, and adjusted free cash flow came in at $1.216 billion. Management raised full-year revenue guidance to $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion and adjusted free cash flow guidance to $4.8 billion to $5 billion, and the company holds $10.4 billion in cash and U.S. Treasury securities against just $225.3 million of total debt.
The Street Stays Bullish, Fair Value Does Not
Wall Street is still backing the story. Barclays rates Palantir a Buy with a $273 target, the highest on the Street, while Citi and JPMorgan sit at Buy with targets of $265 and $262. Morgan Stanley and Cantor Fitzgerald rate it a Hold with targets of $233 and $207, and RBC Capital rates the stock a Sell at $130. The median target of $223.43 sits well above the share price, and estimates keep climbing: 19 EPS revisions moved higher over the past 90 days against one lower, putting consensus at $1.82 for fiscal 2026, $2.72 for fiscal 2027, and $4.21 for fiscal 2028.
InvestingPro's Fair Value models take the opposite view, placing intrinsic value at $140.62 per share—10.2% below the current price and far below the Street's median target. On that measure, the pullback has yet to bring Palantir down to fair value.
The main risk is the multiple itself. At 112.1 times EV/EBITDA, the stock is priced for growth to hold in every part of the business, and some parts are already lagging—international commercial revenue grew just 21% year-over-year and 1% from the prior quarter to $184 million, total contract value booked rose only 6% to $2.918 billion against 96% revenue growth, and several eight-figure deals were signed at shorter durations than usual. Management also acknowledged capacity constraints—the company cannot yet service all incoming demand. When Palantir beat estimates on November 2, the stock still fell 3.08% in regular trading and another 3.82% after hours.
Before buying a 103x P/E AI software leader, investors must weigh Palantir's accelerating commercial growth against a valuation that leaves no room for a slowdown. Commercial net dollar retention, U.S. government contract timing, and stock-based compensation dilution are detailed inside the Palantir Technologies Pro Research Report.
Palantir's third quarter proved that commercial customers, not just governments, now drive its growth. At this multiple, though, the stock needs that growth to hold for years, and the November sell-off showed how quickly the market punishes even a record quarter.
Relying on a single high-multiple AI software stock after the Nasdaq-100's slide into correction leaves capital exposed to sharp multiple compression.
